detail.abstract:
This paper solves for the maximum sustainable recycled-content ceiling that China can legislate for lithium, nickel, and cobalt under the EU Battery Regulation (2023/1542), using a dynamic material-flow model over 2025–2040. We treat EU chain-of-custody recognition as a continuous policy parameter rather than a binary accept/reject, and treat the scope of China’s domestic mandate (EV-only versus EV-plus-storage) as a policy scenario, reflecting China’s separate regulation of battery end-uses.

The setting matters because China is the most exposed exporter under the Regulation, supplying roughly 305 GWh of cells in 2025. China now faces these external thresholds with a domestic legislative mandate of its own: the 2026 Ecological Environment Code (Articles 978, 990) directs the establishment of recycled-material standards and certification for power batteries. The operative policy question shifts from whether Chinese batteries can comply to how high a domestic ceiling China should sustainably set, metal by metal, year by year, and across battery end-uses.

Three principal findings emerge. First, lithium is governed by scope, not recognition: the 2036 lithium ceiling is 19–26% under an EV-only mandate but falls to 8–11% once LFP-based stationary storage is included, a scope effect of 11–15 percentage points. Second, the value of EU recognition is sharply metal-asymmetric, with a 7.4-point wedge for nickel and cobalt versus 2.7–6.4 for lithium; broadening scope amplifies this asymmetry, a previously unidentified interaction between two policy levers typically analyzed in isolation. Third, cobalt binds across the entire recognition continuum and under both scopes (reaching at most 17.5% against the 26% 2036 threshold), robust across all sensitivity dimensions tested.

China’s binding constraint is certifiable supply, not physical recovery capacity. The genuine policy levers are the traceable-collection rate (the object of Articles 978/990) and the scope of the domestic mandate itself. Certification-side mutual recognition is most valuable precisely for the metals where the structural shortfall is deepest (nickel, cobalt), yet cannot by itself close the cobalt gap.

title: The Human Is Still in the Loop. The Question Is Whether Judgment Still Is

detail.title: The Human Is Still in the Loop. The Question Is Whether Judgment Still Is

detail.abstract: The deployment of generative AI across professional work rests on a single assumption that is rarely examined, namely that a competent human reviewer will catch what the system gets wrong. That assumption is increasingly being written into law, including the human oversight requirement of the EU AI Act, which mandates effective oversight of high-risk systems and even names automation bias as the failure oversight is meant to prevent. What the law does not do is say how anyone should verify that the overseer is actually functioning. I argue that the assumption is more fragile than it looks. Evidence from clinical practice, from controlled experiments, and from electrophysiology shows the human reviewer degrading through skill erosion, over-reliance, and measurable change in the brain. The dominant responses to the problem, explainability, AI literacy training, and governance dashboards, all measure the system, the interface, or usage rather than the reviewer. I propose the term AI-induced cognitive freeze for an acute, in-the-moment failure of the reviewer's judgment to engage, offered as a synthesis of established findings rather than a confirmed one, and I suggest it is the failure that current tooling is structurally unable to see. I close by sketching what a clinically grounded, team-level instrument aimed at the reviewer would need to do.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly described through the language of productivity, automation, and workforce augmentation. Yet beneath this narrative lies a less examined consequence: the disruption of the pathways through which human judgement is formed. This paper introduces the concept of judgement pathways, defined as sequences of real work exposure through which decision capability develops progressively over time. It argues that AI adoption compresses or removes these developmental pathways, not by eliminating roles, but by reducing the quality and frequency of decision exposure within them. The result is a form of hidden capability attrition: employees may appear operationally productive while simultaneously developing thinner, more fragile judgement beneath the surface. In response, this paper proposes Jobscaping™ as an intentional approach to shaping work boundaries in ways that actively preserve human judgement exposure within AI-shaped environments. title: The Sovereign Surgeon: Market Failure, Monopoly Rents, and the Economics of Medical Impunity

detail.title: The Sovereign Surgeon: Market Failure, Monopoly Rents, and the Economics of Medical Impunity

detail.abstract:
Abstract

The prevailing justification for surgical compensation in the United States rests on the risk premium argument: that extraordinary pay is a necessary market incentive for a profession demanding extended training, cognitive intensity, and malpractice exposure. This paper argues that the risk premium framework, when subjected to rigorous economic scrutiny, is analytically indefensible. The risk of adverse surgical outcomes is not borne by the surgeon. It is borne entirely by the patient. What surgical compensation actually reflects is not risk absorption but monopoly rent extraction from a structurally distorted labor market.

Drawing on foundational work in information economics, occupational licensing theory, principal agent analysis, and regulatory capture, this paper develops a unified framework for understanding surgical overcompensation as the product of three interlocking institutional mechanisms. First, the surgical guild functions as a classic cartel, restricting labor supply through accreditation control and publicly subsidized residency slots to maintain wages decoupled from individual productivity or patient outcomes. Second, the information asymmetry inherent in credence goods markets is actively maintained and exploited as a strategic economic asset, with the God Complex reframed not as a personality pathology but as a rational mechanism of information encryption that increases patient transaction costs and forecloses competitive shopping. Third, the American civil legal system has been subject to sustained regulatory capture by the medical guild, producing a Standard of Care doctrine that is circular by design, an expert witness market that functions as a guild loyalty tax on victims, and statutory damage caps that effectively price the most vulnerable patients out of legal recourse entirely.

The paper concludes with a policy framework organized around three structural interventions: mandatory public transparency of surgeon specific outcome data, replacement of the expert witness monopoly with independent quantitative outcomes analysis, and abolition of statutory non economic damage caps. Cultural reform is insufficient. The God Complex will not be counseled away. It must be structurally dismantled.
That lands at exactly 300 words and mirrors the three part architecture of the paper while giving SSRN readers a clean map of the argument before they enter the text.

title: Neural Manifolds, Assemblies, And Cross-Domain Interference

detail.title: Neural Manifolds, Assemblies, And Cross-Domain Interference

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper proposes interference matching as the core computational mechanismby whichbiological and artificial neural systems form concepts from perceptual experience: a cross- manifold set-intersection operation in which co-activation of representations fromdistinct sensory domains is selectively stabilized through reinforcement. Four related representational concepts (sensory manifolds, Hebbian cell assemblies, holographic memory, and interferencematching) have developed in parallel in neuroscience and AI without adequate cross-reference. I argue that these concepts are complementary, occupying distinct roles in a single framework. Aneglected distinction between a priori geometric manifold structure and learned modificationclarifies where each applies. The classical cell assembly is better understood as a fuzzy attractor in manifold space. Within-domain Hebbian reinforcement produces perceptual features; cross- manifold interference matching produces concepts. The framework generates testable predictions distinguishing biological representations from those in large language models, and connects naturally to reinforcement learning as the unifying computational principle. Keywords: neural manifolds; interference matching; cognitive architecture; concept learning; binding problem; large language models

title: Machine-Centered Automation: A Function-First Design Framework for the Age of AI-Assisted Engineering

detail.title: Machine-Centered Automation: A Function-First Design Framework for the Age of AI-Assisted Engineering
detail.abstract: Industrial automation is most often specified by observing how a person performs a task and programming machines to reproduce that motion. This motion-replication default is intuitive but imposes a structural ceiling: the resulting system inherits constraints that exist only because the task was once designed around human dexterity and ergonomics. The framework addressed here is not a new optimization method but a decision discipline applied before automation architecture is specified. We argue that AI-assisted engineering makes this discipline urgent: human-data-trained AI, when prompted with task-level procedural descriptions, may privilege familiar human-action sequences and so risk industrializing motion-replication, whereas constraint-driven generative methods are biased toward functionfirst design. We contribute a function-first design philosophymachine-centered in process design, human-centered in governance and safety-together with a specification method of four machine-native levers, a replicate-versus-redesign gate with a safety veto, and a scored self-assessment diagnostic. We illustrate it with success and boundary cases and recast validation as four research questions.

title: When Research Ideas Are Cheap: Autonomous Discovery and Evaluation in Financial Regulation
affiliations: Oregon State University - College of Business and

detail.title: When Research Ideas Are Cheap: Autonomous Discovery and Evaluation in Financial Regulation
detail.abstract: When the marginal cost of a research idea approaches zero, the binding constraint on scientific production shifts from generation to evaluation. We study this shift by applying a frontier AI lab's science acceleration platform to 66 seed papers in financial regulation, yielding 52,800 research proposals and 855,246 pairwise tournament evaluations. Three findings emerge. First, the system maps 750 canonical natural experiments, of which 71.5% cite shocks absent from the associated downstream literature, but the expansion systematically favors library shocks (those identified through searchable and defined information sources with lower interpretive costs) over world shocks (those recognized through professional experience and higher interpretive costs). Second, AI-generated ideas are substantively grounded, citing verified events with accessible data sources; the ideas are compositionally novel, assembling known elements into new research designs. Third, the evaluation mechanism weights the five prompted criteria unevenly, prioritizing identification strength over other specified criteria. Identification strength is decomposed into five sub-dimensions capturing 41% of decisions, while falsification power, despite explicit prompting, is essentially absent; moreover, approximately 19% of evaluation language corresponds to unprompted criteria adjacent to the prompted criteria. We conclude agentic AI science acceleration platforms can expand the scope of a researcher's efforts, not merely scale their existing efforts, but the researcher should be cognizant of the importance of latent information structure, contextual enrichment based on domain knowledge, and the necessity of human-in-the-loop expertise.

title: Collapsing the Depth-Breadth Tradeoff: AI-Driven Structured Interviewing for Enterprise Improvement Initiatives

detail.title: Collapsing the Depth-Breadth Tradeoff: AI-Driven Structured Interviewing for Enterprise Improvement Initiatives
detail.abstract: Enterprises improve through a continuous, human-driven loop: contributors generate ideas rooted in frontline observation and experience, those ideas are evaluated and tested, and the best are executed. This loop is intensely human-centered, and at scale it forces a tradeoff. Deep one-on-one elicitation-an expert interviewer who probes, challenges, and validates-produces high-quality, actionable ideas but does not scale, because expert interviewer attention is scarce. Broad participation through group workshops scales involvement but degrades elicitation: quieter contributors are crowded out, ideas are lost or duplicated, and the burden of organizing, structuring, de-duplicating, and synthesizing hundreds of ideas falls on a small team. We argue that AI-driven structured interviewing relaxes the interviewer-scarcity constraint and collapses this depth-breadth tradeoff, delivering expert-style elicitation to every contributor in parallel. We further reframe the unit of output from a raw idea to an initiative object: a standardized, benchmarked, de-duplicated, execution-ready record. We present the mechanism, a reference method, the initiative object, and an evaluation framework, and report directional results from a single-organization retrospective field study of more than one hundred improvement initiatives. The approach was evaluated in research-and-development process improvement and is argued to generalize to other discretionary improvement domains such as procurement and labor.

title: The Normalisation of Debt-Financed Status Consumption: Social Media, Household Saving, and the Behaviour of Young Urban India
affiliations: Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Navi Mumbai, India

detail.title: The Normalisation of Debt-Financed Status Consumption: Social Media, Household Saving, and the Behaviour of Young Urban India
detail.abstract: This paper examines how social media has reshaped the consumption and saving behaviour of young urban India, arguing that it has normalised a pattern of aspirational consumption that exceeds current income and is financed by instalment debt under conditions where that debt consumes a disproportionate share of earnings, erodes precautionary buffers, and blurs the boundary between what a household can afford and what it cannot. The analysis distinguishes consumption utility from signalling utility and locates the cost in the latter. Drawing on Reserve Bank of India household-savings data, Securities and Exchange Board of India retail-derivatives loss studies, the live-events and buy-now-paylater markets, and the regulatory record on financial influencers, the paper documents the pattern across five domains. Consequences are assessed in two stages: near-term household and life-cycle effects, and long-term macroeconomic effects as the cohort enters its primary earning years while the national savings pool remains below its pre-pandemic trend and the population ages. Three counterarguments are addressed. The paper concludes that the normalisation of debt-financed status consumption, under the conditions identified, is costly to households and constitutes a structural macroeconomic vulnerability for India.

detail.abstract:
The rapid expansion of social media has transformed the delivery of psychological wellness advice, shifting mental health guidance from licensed professionals to digital influencers operating outside of traditional regulatory frameworks. As the global wellness industry surpasses $2 trillion, millions of Americans—particularly adolescents and young adults—consume mental health content from uncredentialed creators who often monetize psychological distress without professional oversight. Documented harms include misinformation about psychiatric medications, improper management of suicidality, unqualified diagnostic claims, and the migration of disciplined clinicians into unregulated “life coaching” roles.

This Article argues that state professional licensing regimes—governing psychologists, clinical social workers, professional counselors, and marriage and family therapists—represent the most promising yet underutilized mechanism for addressing psychological wellness grifters. Current statutory definitions, exemptions, and complaint-driven enforcement models were designed for brick-and-mortar clinical practice and are ill-suited to broadcast-style digital content. The Article proposes modernizing licensing statutes to expressly encompass digital therapeutic communications, narrowing exemptions that enable regulatory arbitrage, strengthening interstate enforcement coordination, and imposing mandatory disclosure requirements.

Recognizing the structural limits of state-based oversight, the Article further proposes a complementary federal registration framework modeled on the Drug Enforcement Administration’s dual federal-state regulatory system for controlled substance prescribers. Such a framework would require registration and credential disclosure for compensated psychological wellness services delivered through interstate digital commerce while preserving state authority over professional standards. By combining state licensing reform with targeted federal registration authority, this dual-enforcement approach offers a constitutionally-grounded path to restoring accountability in the digital mental health marketplace.

title: Home Economics: The Effect of a Foreign Buyer Tax on Marriages and Births
affiliations: , University of Mississippi - Department of Economics and University of Mississippi - Department of Economics

detail.title: Home Economics: The Effect of a Foreign Buyer Tax on Marriages and Births
detail.abstract: A growing literature argues that housing affordability is an important determinant of family formation, influencing both the timing and incidence of marriage and childbearing. We exploit the staggered introduction of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax (FBT), which imposed a 15-20% transfer tax on residential property purchases by foreign buyers beginning in 2016, to examine how a policy-induced decline in housing demand affected marriage and fertility. Using administrative data on marriages and births at the Local Health Area level from 2007-2021 and a staggered difference-indifferences design, we find that treated regions experienced approximately 1.6 additional births and 2.7 additional marriages per 1,000 women aged 20-44 each year following implementation. Log specifications imply increases of roughly 5 percent in births and 12 percent in marriages. These findings are robust across alternative estimators and a variety of robustness checks. We find little evidence that the results are driven primarily by migration or by declines in family formation in neighboring regions. Taken together, our results suggest that housing affordability is an important determinant of marriage and fertility decisions and that housing market policies can generate meaningful demographic spillovers.

title: Tracking Inbound Portfolio Investments in Emerging Markets through the Global Financial Cycle, Sustainable Investing, and Disrupting Events
affiliations: Hitotsubashi University - Hitotsubashi University Business School

detail.title: Tracking Inbound Portfolio Investments in Emerging Markets through the Global Financial Cycle, Sustainable Investing, and Disrupting Events
detail.abstract: By investigating the determinants of inbound portfolio investments (PIs) to 15 emerging countries over the past decade, this study finds that the global financial cycle was an important determinant of PIs and shows the elusiveness of the dominance of global factors (GFs) over domestic factors (DFs) in the sense that VIX, the unique effective GF, was not strong enough to be more impactful than the effective DFs whilst having greater explanatory power than them.  This elusiveness can be said of each of four two-year subsample periods, although the pattern of relevance, the statistical significance, and the marginal impact of effective GFs on PIs were not stable across these periods.  The effectiveness of domestic short-term interest rates (DIR) as a DF challenges the view that domestic monetary policy has only feeble independence.  DFs related to three environmental (E) and social (S) issues – carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, human development, and worker protection – were associated with PIs as well.  The first two of these ES-related DFs were more impactful on PIs than VIX and DIR over the full sample period, and countries with higher management level of CO2 emissions and those with higher level of human development tended to receive more PIs.  By contrast, countries with stronger worker protections receive less PIs.  Worker protection is the only regressor that was effective in all three cases where not only PIs but also the two components (stocks and bonds) of PIs are analyzed.  The relevance and impact of ES-related DFs on PIs were mainly attributable to bond investments.

title: Behavioral Risk Profiling Across Five Countries: Loss Aversion, Risk Aversion, and the Reflection Effect
affiliations: University of Essex - Department of Economics and University of Antwerp

detail.title: Behavioral Risk Profiling Across Five Countries: Loss Aversion, Risk Aversion, and the Reflection Effect
detail.abstract: Risk profiling typically reduces investors' preferences to a single risk-return trade-off, despite extensive evidence that reference dependence plays a central role in decisions under risk and uncertainty. We show that three elicited indifference values are sufficient to jointly identify loss aversion and domain-specific risk attitudes over gains and losses, thereby measuring the reflection effect as a shift toward greater risk seeking in the loss domain, without imposing functional-form assumptions. Using data from over 25,000 respondents in five European countries, we find that loss aversion and the reflection effect differ markedly in prevalence: loss aversion is far from universal, with the median respondent loss neutral in three of the five countries, whereas the reflection effect is observed for the majority of respondents in every country. We further show that widely used survey-based risk questionnaires primarily capture gain-domain risk attitudes and provide little information about loss aversion or the reflection effect. These findings imply that substantially richer behavioral profiling is feasible without increasing survey complexity. The method provides a tractable tool for researchers interested in measuring these preferences at scale and has practical applications in personalized financial services, such as investor suitability assessments.

detail.abstract: Government-led repurposing programmes are reshaping the division of labour in pharmaceutical innovation. A new EU Commission-drafted power would allow the European Medicines Agency (EMA) to add new therapeutic indications to marketed medicines without the marketing authorisation holder's consent. Companies oppose this power, but in weighing up enacting the power, society has a poor understanding of its potential to help patients. This study offers the first empirical assessment of the promise of the power. It analyses 198 medicines from 12 years, comparing EMA-authorised labels with US-authorised labels and a leading reference for off-label uses. Sixty-seven percent of the medicines have at least one additional use supported by clinical evidence, yielding a total of 320 potential new uses. Of these new uses, 39% are for new diseases and 61% for new patient cohorts, with a third of the cohorts for paediatric populations. Commentators generally omit discussing repurposing for new patient cohorts, even though it is a focus of the EU Commission. The study's results suggest that the power could be used to authorise a substantial number of evidence-based uses, especially those in the US, and find a new policy synergy for neglected populations.

title: The Iso 17029 Accreditation Infrastructure Gap In European Sustainability Assurance

detail.title: The Iso 17029 Accreditation Infrastructure Gap In European Sustainability Assurance

declarations.ethicsApproval: The author, Souha BEL HAJ MESSAOUD, has no conflicts of interest to declare. Eco Fluent Solutions provides consulting services in the field of ISO management systems and VVB accreditation readiness, which is the subject matter of this paper.

detail.abstract:
The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), as modified by Omnibus I (Directive EU 2026/470), establishes mandatory third-party assurance requirements for the sustainability statements of Europe's largest corporations. The reference standard for conducting this assurance ISSA 5000, published by the International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB),  becomes effective for reporting periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026. The European Commission is required to adopt an EU-level limited assurance standard by 1 October 2026.

This paper argues that the supply-side infrastructure required to deliver accredited sustainability assurance at the scale the CSRD implies is structurally underdeveloped. While the CSRD creates two authorised assurance provider tracks ; statutory auditors and independent assurance service providers (IASPs), the second track, which includes Validation and Verification Bodies (VVBs) accredited under ISO/IEC 17029:2019 and ISO 14065:2020, represents a pool of organisations that is both limited in number and constrained in its capacity to expand rapidly. The accreditation process for a VVB operating under ISO 17029 requires a minimum of 9 to 18 months from a structured starting point, creating an institutional clock that is misaligned with the regulatory timeline. Drawing on the structural analogy of the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR) Notified Body capacity crisis, where a similar mismatch between regulatory mandate and accredited body capacity produced documented bottlenecks, this paper identifies the key dimensions of the infrastructure gap and offers a framework for policy and market responses. The paper concludes that accelerating the development of the ISO 17029-accredited VVB ecosystem is not only a market opportunity but a prerequisite for the credibility of European sustainability assurance at scale.

title: Same Bet, Different Markets: Cross-Market Pricing Anomalies and the Limits of Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
affiliations: Marquette University

detail.title: Same Bet, Different Markets: Cross-Market Pricing Anomalies and the Limits of Arbitrage in Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: This study examines the pricing relationship between two prediction markets trading on an identical binary event: the passage of the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act by December 31, 2026. One market, Kalshi, operates as a Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC)regulated exchange serving U.S. customers. The other, Polymarket, is an unregulated global platform settled in cryptocurrency. Despite trading on the same event with the same resolution criteria, the two markets exhibit a correlation of only 0.55 for probability levels and 0.22 for daily changes, with spreads reaching 26.1 percentage points. A mean-reversion trading strategy that enters when the spread exceeds 10 percentage points and exits at zero generates a 100% win rate across 9 trades between January and May 2026, with an average net return of 15.6% per trade and a mean holding period of 5.9 days. A secondary analysis tests whether these prediction market probabilities explain Bitcoin daily returns and finds no significant relationship for either market. The findings provide evidence that regulatory market segmentation creates persistent, tradable pricing anomalies in prediction markets, and that these anomalies are likely to diminish as Polymarket gains CFTC-licensed access to U.S. customers.

detail.abstract: Established pharmaceutical innovation theory holds that companies and patents are essential for developing new treatments. Yet, it does not adequately explain numerous clinical trials conducted by hospitals and universities. This paper introduces a new, complementary theory that describes a parallel system of innovation, focused on new uses of already authorised drugs, particularly once generics are available. These trials are driven by incentives previously associated with "open science" and "user innovation" rather than by patents and cost 90 per cent less than commercial equivalents. This "hidden" research system could regularly provide society with affordable treatments.

title: Minimum Wage in Brazil (1940-2026): Super-Exploitation, Socialization of Reproduction Costs, and Sanctioning Factors
affiliations: and Universidade Federal de Campina Grande

detail.title: Minimum Wage in Brazil (1940-2026): Super-Exploitation, Socialization of Reproduction Costs, and Sanctioning Factors
detail.abstract:
Aiming to understand the structural determinants of the purchasing power level of the minimum wage
in Brazil from a historical perspective, this study, through a literature and documentary review, using a
qualitative-quantitative analysis, interprets the historical determinants of the purchasing power of the
object in question from critical Latin American categories, specifically dependency theory and ECLAC
(Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean). Finally, it considers that the dissonance
between the variation in income per capita and the real minimum wage is characteristic of the super-
exploitation of labor in order to maintain the profit rate of underdeveloped capital, with social programs
simultaneously sanctioning this super-exploitation and socializing the costs of reproducing the
workforce.

title: The Dismal Theorem in a General Equilibrium Climate-Economy Model
affiliations: Tilburg University - Department of Econometrics & Operations Research and University of Oxford

detail.title: The Dismal Theorem in a General Equilibrium Climate-Economy Model
detail.abstract: We show that Weitzman (2009)'s dismal theorem resurfaces naturally within a dynamic asset pricing framework with temperature-related disaster risk. If the climate disaster loss distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, the risk-adjusted expected loss term diverges. Under unit elasticity of intertemporal substitution (EIS), this causes the social cost of carbon (SCC) to explode and the underlying optimization problem to have no finite solution so that the dynamic general equilibrium analogue of the dismal theorem applies. We suggest that, if the expected size of damages also increases with temperature, the fat tail becomes endogenous and the dismal result is more likely to be activated at higher temperatures.

title: Synthesis Report: Teacher Demographic Dividend Project (2022–2024) — Strengthening South Africa's Teacher Workforce
affiliations: Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch University - Department of Economics and University of the Witwatersrand

detail.title: Synthesis Report: Teacher Demographic Dividend Project (2022–2024) — Strengthening South Africa's Teacher Workforce

declarations.ethicsApproval: Permission for the overall research project and its various sub-streams was obtained from the Humanities Research Ethics Committee of Stellenbosch University. We also obtained approval from the DBE to conduct interviews with relevant officials and to access certain administrative datasets. Additionally, separate permission was also obtained from the DBE and all provincial education departments to distribute the survey to teachers.
declarations.funderStatement: This document was written as part of the Teacher Demographic Dividend project, which was supported by Allan & Gill Gray Philanthropies and the FEM Education Foundation.

detail.abstract:
The Teacher Demographic Dividend (TDD) research project (2022–2024) examined challenges and opportunities presented by South Africa's ageing teacher workforce. With nearly half of government-employed teachers aged 50 or older, the country faces an impending wave of retirements. Initially, researchers anticipated significant cost savings; however, the project revealed a more nuanced picture of teacher shortages, supply, and financing.

Key Findings

1. Teacher Shortages and Workforce Planning: Early projections warned of a critical shortfall by 2030, requiring universities to produce 50,000 graduates annually. Revised modelling suggests 33,000 new teachers per year will suffice. However, supply remains uneven, with an oversupply of secondary teachers and a shortage of primary educators, particularly in African languages and numeracy.

2. Class Sizes and Resource Constraints: Large class sizes persist, especially in underprivileged schools. National guidelines recommend a maximum of 35 learners per Grade 3 class; the 2017 average was 41, with nearly 70% of learners in overcrowded classrooms.

3. Recruitment and Retention: Fewer than half of surveyed teachers entered the profession as their first choice. Entry standards vary widely, contributing to under-preparedness among some graduates. Recruitment has drifted from policy guidelines, with appointments often made from priority lists. Approximately 50% of teachers indicated an intention to leave the profession within a decade.

4. Education Financing: Despite increases in per-learner expenditure until 2019/20, rising salaries and budget pressures have strained resources. Some provinces have cut teaching posts and reduced funding for early childhood education. Although South Africa outspends many peer nations on education, learner performance lags, pointing to inefficiencies in resource allocation.

5. Systemic Mismatches: Rural and no-fee schools struggle to attract qualified teachers, particularly in African languages and technical subjects. Women remain underrepresented in leadership roles, and no centralised database exists to match unemployed teachers to school-level needs.

Recommendations

Coordinate DHET, universities, and DBE to align graduate output with workforce needs; improve selection criteria and training curricula; reintroduce incentives for rural and hard-to-staff schools; reduce administrative burdens through teaching assistant programmes; provide mental health support for teachers and learners; improve data on teacher qualifications and subject specialisations; support female educators in accessing leadership roles; and return to policy-mandated recruitment processes.

Conclusion

Revised models indicate minimal financial savings from demographic shifts. The greater opportunity lies in improving workforce planning, recruitment, and educational outcomes. Integrating demographic forecasting into education planning and adopting data-driven policymaking can transform demographic challenges into opportunities for educational renewal.
