detail.abstract: Carbon-price volatility poses a major barrier to the timely investment in low-carbon technologies. Carbon Contracts for Difference (CCfDs) have recently attracted attention as a policy instrument that mitigates carbon-price risk by providing revenue guarantees. This study examines the role of CCfDs within a real options framework under carbon price uncertainty. We derive optimal investment thresholds with and without a CCfD and analyze how carbon-price volatility, strike-price design, and technological characteristics affect investment timing. Numerical results show that CCfDs accelerate low-carbon investment by reducing exposure to downside carbon-price risk, with stronger effects under higher volatility, higher strike prices, and lower emission factors after investment. Monte Carlo simulations further indicate that CCfDs increase the expected project value while improving downside-risk profiles. These findings provide quantitative insights into the design of CCfDs to support low-carbon investment under carbon-price uncertainty.

title: Fixed Payoffs, Floating Prices: Self-fulfilling Bubbles in on-chain Prediction Markets

detail.title: Fixed Payoffs, Floating Prices: Self-fulfilling Bubbles in on-chain Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: We show that overpricing in on-chain prediction markets is self-fulfilling: for the same fundamentals, a bubble and a no-bubble equilibrium coexist. The bubble survives only for longshots, and a global-games refinement selects a unique tipping point. The cause is institutional. A one-dollar cap and a two-sided market seem to let a contrarian short an overpriced contract via the complementary token, but that short is fully collateralized with no credit, so disciplining a longshot ties up nearly a dollar and invites a squeeze, making discipline a coordination problem. Capital-weighted clearing underprices favorites. We prove uniqueness and identify levers that restore discipline.

title: The Implementability of Contextual Coordination

detail.title: The Implementability of Contextual Coordination
detail.abstract: We study coordination observed across multiple implementation contexts. A contextcontingent coordination dataset is classically implementable if its observed marginals can be embedded in one joint probability law over all potential context outcomes. This global-coupling condition is satisfied by hidden-type models, common-prior signal structures, classical mediators, recommendation devices, and correlated-equilibrium mechanisms. In the canonical two-agent, two-context, binary-outcome environment, it is equivalent to the Bell-CHSH/Fine inequalities, so the bound |S| ≤ 2 is a revealed restriction of classical probability rather than a physical assumption. We then introduce coherent implementation systems, represented by density matrices and context measurements that need not be jointly diagonalizable. These systems generate a strictly larger implementability region, bounded in the binary benchmark by Tsirelson's inequality, |S| ≤ 2 √ 2. The constructive counterpart is a context-sensitive mediation device: an institution prepares a readiness state, applies the test associated with the realized context, and sends recommendations that satisfy context-contingent obedience constraints. The distinction is welfare-relevant when continuation value depends on compatibility, timing, interoperability, legal consistency, or reconfiguration across modes. The framework does not claim that economies are physically quantum. It gives a revealed-implementability test for when classical probability is sufficient and when coordination requires a coherent institutional representation.

title: How Egyptian Manufacturing SMEs Can Protect Working Capital During Inflation?
affiliations: German University in Cairo (GUC), Cairo, Egyp and German University in Cairo

detail.title: How Egyptian Manufacturing SMEs Can Protect Working Capital During Inflation?
detail.abstract: This study examines how Egyptian manufacturing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) endured and adapted to the severe inflationary period of 2022-2024. Using an integrated mixedmethods approach that combines qualitative interviews with multiple case studies, the research identifies, analyzes, and validates practical strategies that enhance SME financial resilience during periods of acute macroeconomic instability. The study extends theoretical understanding of SME resilience under macroeconomic crises by integrating dynamic capabilities, working capital management, and inflation adaptation into a unified framework tailored to emerging markets. It contributes localized, evidence-based insights to the business administration literature, demonstrating how firm-level agility can mitigate systemic inflationary pressures. From a managerial perspective, the findings provide a tested strategic roadmap for SME owners and financial managers to strengthen liquidity management, optimize fixed-cost allocation, and sustain profitability throughout inflationary cycles. For policymakers and financial institutions, the study highlights the need for structural reforms to improve SME access to foreign currency, affordable credit, and energy-efficiency investments. The research concludes that inflation, while inevitable, can be effectively managed through coordinated micro-level strategies that safeguard liquidity, stabilize working capital, and protect profitability. By transforming inflation from an uncontrollable external shock into a navigable economic reality, Egyptian manufacturing SMEs can sustain productivity, preserve employment, and contribute to national economic stability.

title: Federated Reinforcement Learning-based Energy Trading Optimization in Smart Microgrids

detail.title: Federated Reinforcement Learning-based Energy Trading Optimization in Smart Microgrids
detail.abstract: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) and the decentralization of power grids necessitate robust, privacy-preserving energy trading mechanisms for smart microgrids. Traditional centralized optimization methods expose sensitive user data and suffer from single points of failure. This paper proposes a novel Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) framework for optimizing peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading in smart microgrids. The framework combines the privacy-preserving properties of federated learning with the sequential decision-making capabilities of deep reinforcement learning (DRL). Using a simulated microgrid environment with 100 prosumers, we compare the proposed FRL model against three baselines: independent DRL, centralized DRL, and a rule-based trading system. Results indicate that the FRL model achieves a 23.4% reduction in overall energy costs, a 15.7% decrease in grid dependency, and maintains a privacy score of 0.96 (where 1 is perfect privacy) over 500 training rounds. The model also demonstrates robust resilience to node dropouts, maintaining 89% efficiency even when 30% of nodes are offline. These findings suggest that FRL offers a scalable, secure, and efficient solution for decentralized energy markets.

title: Mind the G(a)ap: Non-GAAP Disclosure and Credibility Perceptions among German Investors
affiliations: , TU Dortmund University and Technical University of Dortmund

detail.title: Mind the G(a)ap: Non-GAAP Disclosure and Credibility Perceptions among German Investors
detail.abstract: This study experimentally examines how the disclosure of non-GAAP measures influences perceived disclosure credibility among professional and non-professional investors in Germany. Motivated by IFRS 18, which introduces guidance on the presentation of Management Performance Measures (MPMs), we investigate whether a perception gap exists between these investor groups regarding the credibility of a firm´s reporting. Building on attribution theory and the concept of the expectation gap, we find that professional investors remain largely unaffected by non-GAAP disclosures, whereas non-professional investors view reports, including non-GAAP measures, as significantly more credible than stand-alone GAAPbased reports. We conclude that non-GAAP measures help reducing an existing perception gap from annual reports containing only GAAP measures. While our findings highlight the need to better address the information needs of non-professional investors by extending disclosures beyond GAAP-measures, our results also stress the potential vulnerability of non-professional investors to strategically framed disclosures, emphasizing the need for regulatory efforts to enhance the transparency of financial reporting.

title:
Diverged Growth Paths of Europe:
Comparative Analysis on the Development of Ireland and Spain
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
Diverged Growth Paths of Europe:
Comparative Analysis on the Development of Ireland and Spain
detail.abstract: This paper answers the question of "why are some countries rich and others poor?" in a more subtle context. While most studies focus on the economic differences between LICs and HICs, this paper delves into the two countries that earn high incomes by world standards, but diverge in their economic growth rates. On the surface, Ireland and Spain both have large economies and are considered wealthy nations on the continent. To uncover the embedded causes of economic disparities, the paper first examines and compares economic indices and macroeconomic performances, primarily using data from the World Bank's World Development Indicators (WDI) database. Then, the Solow Growth Model is utilized to validate the divergence between the two countries' growth and visualize it. Through a comparative analysis, this paper recommends macroeconomic policies and strategies for Spain. These recommendations can be extended to other large economies with slow growth rates.

title: Privacy-preserving Energy Management in Microgrid Trading Networks using Federated Reinforcement Learning

detail.title: Privacy-preserving Energy Management in Microgrid Trading Networks using Federated Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: The integration of distributed energy resources (DERs) into microgrid trading networks introduces significant privacy and security challenges for traditional centralized energy management systems. This paper proposes a novel framework that combines federated learning (FL) with reinforcement learning (RL) to enable privacy-preserving, decentralized energy trading among microgrid participants. Unlike conventional approaches that require sharing raw consumption and production data with a central coordinator, our federated reinforcement learning (FedRL) architecture allows local agents to learn optimal bidding and scheduling policies while sharing only encrypted model updates. Using a simulated microgrid network of 50 prosumers over 12 months, we demonstrate that FedRL achieves 94.2% of the efficiency of a centralized RL oracle while reducing data exposure by over 99%. Our results indicate convergence within 150 communication rounds, with an average privacy leakage score of 0.018 (scale 0-1). The framework shows robust performance under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data distributions and intermittent communication failures. These findings suggest that FedRL offers a viable path toward scalable, privacy-compliant energy markets aligned with GDPR and emerging data protection regulations.

title: Emergence via Phase Transitions: Mechanism Landscapes and Universal Convergence across Complex Systems
affiliations: Clevix AI Research

detail.title: Emergence via Phase Transitions: Mechanism Landscapes and Universal Convergence across Complex Systems
detail.abstract:
Why do independently trained neural networks converge to the same internal representations [37, 23]? Why does grokking-sudden generalisation after memorisation-follow universal statistics across architectures and tasks [42]? Why do independent evolutionary lineages repeatedly arrive at the same metabolic solutions across 993 yeast species [38]? We propose a candidate explanation for a structural motif common to these phenomena: when a system's energy budget crosses a critical threshold Ec, competing mechanisms undergo a phase transition that drives convergence toward a unique fixed point determined by the system's physical constraint set P. We do not claim to explain all emergence, but to identify a recurring phase-transition structure across convergence phenomena in learning, biology, and physics. Concisely: many emergence phenomena can be understood as phase transitions in mechanism landscapes under physical and informational constraints. 

      We formalise this structural motif as the Hierarchical Emergence Framework (HEF), specified by a six-tuple (R (1) , L, A0, G, mode, E) together with P = (P thermo , P info , Φ), where the translation map Φ is an order-isomorphism of constraint lattices grounded in Landauer's Principle and the Jarzynski Equality. Three theorems follow. The Physical Feasibility Theorem guarantees that all generated entities satisfy thermodynamic and information-theoretic constraints simultaneously. The Energy-Diversity Theorem establishes a phase transition at Ec between an exploration regime and a convergence regime. Universal Feature Convergence then follows via the Banach Fixed-Point Theorem: any two HEF instances sharing P and operating below Ec converge to the same fixed-point representations, independent of initial conditions. A Causal Emergence Theorem additionally shows that the fixed point R∞ has strictly higher Effective Information [21] than the micro-level R (1) , with the gain bounded by a measurable training-dynamics quantity. 

      We validate HEF empirically through 111 grokking experiments (p ∈ {23, 31, 41, 53, 67, 83, 97}, λ ∈ {1, 2}, multiple seeds). Universal Convergence is confirmed : all grokked models converge to 0.9745±0.014 regardless of p, λ, or training fraction (ANOVA p > 0.13; CV= 1.47%). A novel Ec fingerprint is identified: the weight norm ∥w∥ 2 peaks ∼1,050 steps before grokking in 92% of runs, tracing the threephase HEF trajectory. Accuracy curves collapse onto a tanh kink (R 2 = 0.93), placing grokking in the Landau-Ginzburg mean-field universality class. G2 scaling ∆t ∝ 1/(frac • p • λ) is supported across seven primes (β =-1.39 ± 0.20, R 2 = 0.91). 

     HEF makes three falsifiable cross-domain predictions: (P1) anaerobic yeast lineages have higher genomic convergence than aerobic lineages at the same phylogenetic distance; (P2) LLMs trained with higher weight decay produce representations with higher causal potency; (P3) a critical weight-decay threshold λc(p) ∈ (2, 4) exists beyond which grokking fails via mechanism starvation. Code, data, and a diagnostic toolkit (hef-tools) are provided to enable independent replication and application to new systems.

title: Intuitive Cognitive Abilities and Attitudes towards Risk and Ambiguity: An Exploratory Study with Educational Implications
affiliations: and University of Turin

detail.title: Intuitive Cognitive Abilities and Attitudes towards Risk and Ambiguity: An Exploratory Study with Educational Implications
detail.abstract:
This study investigates cognitive mechanisms underlying decisionmaking under uncertainty, focusing on intuitive processing (System 1) and on rapid, non-symbolic numerical cognition captured by Approximate Number System (ANS) tasks. 
     In particular, we hypothesized that individuals with higher System 1 and ANS proficiency are more tolerant of risk and ambiguity, as they tend to be more comfortable and adaptive when making decisions under incomplete information. 
     To test this, we utilized WarmApp, a computerized task designed to isolate System 1 processing through strict time constraints, thereby inhibiting analytical strategies like counting. The task assesses both ANS acuity and visual pattern recognition. 
     Results suggest that individuals with higher System 1 proficiency and ANS acuity are more tolerant of risk and ambiguity. Furthermore, exploratory analysis suggests that training these intuitive abilities may reduce ambiguity aversion, particularly in low-proficiency individuals. 
    These findings contribute to the field of numerical cognition by demonstrating that strengthening the intuitive, non-symbolic processing of quantities can foster the 'propensity to attempt' essential for decision-making in both economic and educational contexts.

title: Is Energy-Only Interconnection Working? Empirical Evidence from Two Decades of US Market Data
affiliations: , Duke University, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab), University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley - Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab)

detail.title: Is Energy-Only Interconnection Working? Empirical Evidence from Two Decades of US Market Data

detail.abstract:
Growth in electricity demand and generation is increasingly constrained by generator interconnection bottlenecks, with 2,061 gigawatts of proposed capacity stalled in US queues. Energy-only, or non-firm, interconnection is intended to let generators connect to the grid more cheaply and quickly by accepting "as-available" service. Texas's "connect and manage" model has made this approach central to reform debates, but most US regions instead offer two service options: firm Network Resource Interconnection Service (NRIS) and non-firm Energy Resource Interconnection Service (ERIS). Using a dataset of over 36,000 interconnection requests and 4,500 cost studies spanning two decades, we show that ERIS fails to function as a true non-firm access option, offering neither cheaper nor faster interconnection. The historical network-upgrade cost discount associated with ERIS is driven by a "threshold effect," providing financial relief only when network upgrades are entirely avoided. Once physical upgrades are triggered, non-firm (ERIS) and firm (NRIS) interconnection face statistically comparable costs. As mounting grid constraints have cut the share of zero-cost ERIS outcomes from 80% to 10%, ERIS's financial and temporal advantages have largely evaporated and developer demand for this service has contracted. Our results suggest that the concept of "energy-only" interconnection is not inherently flawed; rather, ERIS's observed performance stems from restrictive study methodologies that do not reflect the characteristics of a true non-firm service option. These findings point to an opportunity to align interconnection rules with as-available grid access through operational redispatch, and to examine whether capacity value can remain informed by grid constraints without being dictated by interconnection service.

Note: This manuscript is one of two complementary papers on energy-only interconnection. The companion paper reviews the regulatory and institutional design of ERIS and is also available as an SSRN preprint under the title, ‘A Review of United States Energy-only Generator Interconnection Service Policy and Considerations for Reform’, available at: https://ssrn.com/abstract=6870718

detail.abstract:
Abstract

Background: Reaching banking services to all is essential for sustainable development of villages in Bangladesh. Most people live in villages and coastal areas. But due to distance, lack of transportation or infrastructure, and low awareness of digital transactions, a large segment is still outside the banking facilities. Agent banking can overcome these problems of traditional banks as an easy medium. But due to various regulatory barriers, technical problems, and fear in the minds of people, this service is still not fully spread in remote areas.

Objective: The real purpose of this research is to see one thing: how agent banking is helping ordinary people in the villages of Bagerhat to access banking services.The adoption scenario is assessed through Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) Theory. The obstacles like digital illiteracy and infrastructure are explored. The impact of different financial parameters on the poor and marginal coastal community is also evaluated.

Method: This study used primary data and employed a mixed-method research design. A field survey was conducted quantitatively among rural users to measure their satisfaction, perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Qualitative KII with 5 frontline bank agents and higher authorities complemented the analysis and contextualization of the systemic and operational issues. The data collected was analysed to produce behavioural intentions mapping and social network influence on banking adoption.

Result: According to the findings, greater financial access is contributed by agent banking in the form of cheaper, closer, and more convenient deposit, withdrawal and utility bill payment services. Yet, because of digital illiteracy, interface experience of inexperienced users is a major hurdle to independent use. So, they become highly dependent on the physical presence of agents for assistance. Frequent server down and bad internet connection make users unhappy. These problems also reduce their confidence. People talk to each other about these issues, and it makes them doubt the banking system even more.

Conclusion: This study has shown that agent banking is very good for rural and coastal areas of Bangladesh. But the problem is due to the low digital knowledge of people and weak internet. To overcome this problem, the government and banks should provide good internet facilities in villages. At the same time, people need to be taught to use digital banking and more small loans should be given. By doing these things, the barriers within the banks will be reduced and the poor people will be able to transact money easily.

title: Pricing Partisan Identity: Evidence from School Bonds
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Finance, University of Texas at Dallas,  and

detail.title: Pricing Partisan Identity: Evidence from School Bonds
detail.abstract: We study whether security prices respond when the institutions they fund become partisan. We use the staggered adoption of partisan school board elections across North Carolina counties between 2014 and 2024. School bonds in adopting counties are issued at lower yields than school bonds in counties that remain nonpartisan, generating $33 to $45 million in interest savings on post-adoption issuances. North Carolina provides an opportunity to test the mechanism behind this effect. Unlike in most states, its school bonds are backed by the same full-faith-and-credit pledge and county taxing authority as other general obligation bonds the county issues. If the lower yields reflect revised beliefs about county fiscal fundamentals, the effect should appear across all of a county's GO bonds. Instead, non-school bonds issued in adopting counties show no change in offering yields. Because one taxing authority backs both, this within-issuer differential is inconsistent with revised beliefs about credit risk and instead provides novel evidence of the nonpecuniary utility investors derive from holding securities tied to partisan governance. School bond issuance volume does not contract following adoption, ruling out a supply-side explanation.

title: Multimodal Deep Learning Fusion Approaches for Automated Depression Detection: A Systematic Review
affiliations: , American University of Ras Al Khaimah and University of Waterloo

detail.title: Multimodal Deep Learning Fusion Approaches for Automated Depression Detection: A Systematic Review
detail.abstract: Background: Depression affects over 280 million people worldwide, yet diagnosis still depends on subjective clinical interviews and self-report questionnaires that are vulnerable to recall bias, social desirability effects, and limited access to trained professionals. Multimodal deep learning may enable more objective depression detection by combining behavioral, verbal, and physiological signals from multiple data sources. Methods: This systematic review followed the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We searched IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, SpringerLink, and ScienceDirect for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2018 and August 2025. Eligible studies used at least two measured input modalities for depression classification or severity assessment with quantitative evaluation. From an initial pool of 120 records, screening and eligibility assessment yielded 50 included studies. Results: Across clinical, social media, and laboratory settings, multimodal systems outperformed unimodal baselines. Audio-video fusion and electroencephalography combined with facial video or eye tracking produced the largest gains. Alignmentaware audio-text models improved accuracy when reliable timestamps were available. Audio-video pipelines on standard corpora reached precision values near 95%, with sensitivity and specificity frequently above 80%, though metric reporting varied across studies. Accuracy generally plateaued beyond two or three modalities; well-optimized bimodal systems often matched or outperformed larger combinations while remaining easier to deploy. Among fusion strategies, hybrid approaches that combine feature-level and decision-level information most often achieved the highest accuracy and stability, and attention-based or transformer-based fusion added gains in both performance and interpretability. Conclusions: Multimodal deep learning can improve the objectivity of depression assessment, but clinical adoption requires progress on several fronts: standardized evaluation protocols and metrics, transparent handling of temporal alignment and missing modalities, external validation in diverse populations, fairness and uncertainty evaluation, and deployment-oriented research on privacy-preserving and on-device inference. This systematic review was not prospectively registered.

title: From Cost Competitiveness to Bankability: ISRU as a Market Architecture Problem
affiliations: Ecole des Ponts ParisTech

detail.title: From Cost Competitiveness to Bankability: ISRU as a Market Architecture Problem
detail.abstract: Despite sustained technical progress and growing sector-wide investment-global spacetech venture capital reaching $7.8 billion in 2024 [1]-a targeted evidentiary search of selected infrastructure-finance databases (World Bank/IFC PPI, IJGlobal, EIB, and EBRD lending registries, 2015-2026) identified no ISRU extraction-and-processing project that has attracted non-recourse project debt, Development Finance Institution infrastructure loans, or investment-grade capital structured against the cash flows of space resource production. This paper argues that ISRU's commercialisation bottleneck is not well explained by engineering performance or cost competitiveness alone. The missing layer is market architecture that capital can underwrite. Drawing on project finance theory [2,3] , Basel III supervisory slotting criteria [4] as an analytical proxy, transaction cost economics [5] , real options theory [6] , and market design theory [7,8] , this paper proposes the Triple Vacuum diagnostic-three independent structural deficits each argued to be sufficient to block capital-and the Milestone-Monetisation Ladder (MML), a five-stage framework that makes ISRU technical progress legible to infrastructure capital markets at every development stage. The Interlune helium-3 trajectory is examined as an illustrative case consistent with MML Stage 3 dynamics. The framework is presented as a conceptual synthesis requiring empirical validation; it is not an empirical financing study.

title: Context-dependent removal of emerging pollutants in constructed wetlands: a dependence-aware meta-analysis and explainable machine-learning framework for performance envelopes

detail.title: Context-dependent removal of emerging pollutants in constructed wetlands: a dependence-aware meta-analysis and explainable machine-learning framework for performance envelopes
detail.abstract: Constructed wetlands (CWs) are widely used as low-energy polishing systems for wastewater treatment, yet reported removal efficiencies for emerging pollutants (EPs) vary greatly across pollutant classes, wetland configurations, influent matrices, and experimental scales. This limits the transferability of single pooled removal estimates for engineering design. We synthesized 67 peer-reviewed studies, approximately 2.0*104 concentration records, and 841 paired influent-effluent comparisons using multilevel random-effects models with cluster-robust inference. Heterogeneity was extreme (I2 ≈ 99%). Mean lnRR differed strongly by pollutant class, from about -9.1 for microplastics to -2.4, -2.2, and -1.8 for antibiotics, endocrine-disrupting compounds, and persistent organic pollutants, respectively. Horizontally subsurface-flow systems outperformed surface-flow systems (-5.53 vs -1.48). Removal appeared to weaken from laboratory to full scale (-4.21 to -1.72). After false-discovery-rate correction, only wetland area (β = 0.418, p = 0.022) and flow rate (β = 0.380, p = 0.036) remained significant in linear meta-regression, and both effects were weak relative to the residual heterogeneity. A CatBoost model captured nonlinear structure more effectively (R2 = 0.920, RMSE = 1.077); flow rate, influent concentration, wastewater type, temperature, and study scale were the dominant predictors. These results do not support a universal removal coefficient. Instead, they support context-specific performance envelopes, the preferential use of subsurface-flow systems for dissolved EP polishing, conservative translation of laboratory data, and mass-balance verification when particulate removal is inferred

detail.abstract: Trading-strategy evidence is often produced from symbol-date panels, but the tradable object is a date-level portfolio return. Treating selected rows as independent can therefore overstate evidence when same-date rows share market, factor, liquidity, or volatility shocks and when the resulting date returns are serially dependent. This paper proposes a double-robust inference framework for panel trading evidence: date aggregation, HAC-delta inference, and dependent bootstrap resampling jointly address cross-sectional and serial dependence in the date-return series. The main theoretical object is the Sharpe Unified Variance Inflation Factor (Sharpe UVIF), defined as the ratio of the long-run delta-method variance of the date-level Sharpe estimator to the row-pooled IID delta-method variance. It is the Sharperatio analogue of a design effect. A companion Effective Information Rate (EIR) reports the fraction of nominal row-level information that remains nonredundant under an equicorrelation diagnostic. The empirical analysis is a reproducible evaluation of public factor-zoo candidates using Kenneth French and AQR data. The results show that benchmark momentum survives the dependence-aware boundary, while weaker panel claims can lose most of their nominal row-level information once the audit is applied.

title: The National Impact of Startups
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The National Impact of Startups
detail.abstract: The question of whether governments should channel scarce public resources toward innovative startups or toward established traditional businesses is frequently posed as a binary choice. This paper argues that the binary framing is misleading and that the correct answer is conditional on two structural variables: the country's stage of economic development and the size of its population. Drawing on Porter's theory of the stages of national competitive development, World Bank and International Finance Corporation data on small and medium-sized enterprises, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics figures on firm survival, and comparative evidence from South Korea, Israel, India, and Estonia, the study develops an integrated framework. It contends that economies in the factor-and investment-driven stages should prioritize traditional businesses and small and medium-sized enterprises, which generate roughly 90 percent of firms and more than half of global employment, because such economies require broad-based job creation, a stable tax base, and capital accumulation before they can absorb the high failure rates inherent in innovation. As economies mature toward the innovation-driven stage, the marginal returns to traditional expansion diminish and public investment should pivot decisively toward startups and research and development. Population size further conditions this pivot: large-population economies can sustain a domestic-market-led innovation strategy, whereas small advanced economies must pursue an export-first, niche-specialized model. The paper closes with sequenced policy recommendations for matching investment strategy to national circumstances.

title: Mapping risk and protective factors in child welfare investigations: A latent class analysis of assessment profiles
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Karlstad University

detail.title: Mapping risk and protective factors in child welfare investigations: A latent class analysis of assessment profiles
detail.abstract: Background:Child Welfare Services (CWS) assessments in Sweden guide interventions for maltreatment and behavioural problems, but how risk and protective factors interact is poorly understood. Person-oriented studies are rare, limiting evidence-based decision-making.Objective:To identify typologies of risk and protective factors in Swedish CWS investigations and examine their associations with gender, age, municipal segregation, foreign background, and household compositionParticipants and Setting:Retrospective cross-sectional data from 21,184 child welfare investigations were collected from 134 Swedish municipalities and city districts (2023–2024).Methods:Latent class analysis was used to identify typologies. Measurement invariance for gender was assessed. Multinomial logistic regression examined associations between modal class membership and covariates, yielding average marginal effects (AME) with 95% CI.Results:Distinct typologies emerged. Girls were less likely than boys to be found in high maltreatment/low protection (AME=−0.04, 95%CI[−0.04,−0.03]), high criminal behaviour/high parental support (AME=−0.07, 95%CI[−0.07,−0.06]), and moderate parental risk/high protection (AME=−0.02, 95%CI[−0.02,−0.02) typologies. Age increased the likelihood of behavioral problem typologies (AME per year increase: 0.01–0.02, p<0.05). Spatial-income segregation showed negligible influence. Foreign background increased the likelihood of High abuse/moderate protection and resilience (AME=0.05, 95%CI[0.04, 0.06]), No risk (AME=0.06 95%CI[0.04, 0.07]), and High criminal behaviour/high parental support (AME=0.01 95%CI[0.01, 0.02]). Non-two-parent households were more likely to be in adverse typologies (e.g., high neglect/low protection: AME=0.05–0.09, all p<0.05).Conclusions:CWS assessments reveal clear gender and demographic patterns in risk/protection typologies, limited differentiation of behavioral problem subtypes, and possible overreliance on broad parental protective factors. More nuanced, evidence-based assessment tools are needed.

detail.abstract: Developing country governments routinely attempt to collect revenue using threats they cannot systematically enforce. We study how citizens assess the credibility of such empty threats in the context of payment for electricity in Madhya Pradesh, India, where state-run utilities recovered only 60 cents per dollar of power supplied. Using two field experiments covering 30,000 households with high arrears, we show that the household response to a threat depends on the state's choice of messenger. The first experiment randomly exposes households to reminders, threats, and enforcement action without changing incentives, state capacity, laws, or information about debt. Legal threats delivered by local linesmen-state agents with a history of ignoring non-paymenthave no effect. Yet identical notices sent by registered mail, bypassing linesmen, reduce arrears by 11.4 percent among recipients, a 241 percent return-on-investment. We hypothesize that choosing compromised messengers changes household beliefs about the state's credibility, implying dynamic effects that we test with the second experiment: a year later, we randomly mail a legal notice to previously-treated households. Past treatments affect future responses. Consumers originally visited by a linesman do not respond, while those not exposed to linesmen reduce arrears. Moreover, when we increase linesman credibility by requiring them to follow up on threats, this gap narrows. The experimental results are together consistent with a model in which consumers use the state's choice of messenger to infer the threat's credibility, and demonstrate that low-credibility state agents can render threats ineffective. Low-capacity governments may improve revenue collection by bypassing their agents.

title: Legal Gaps in the EU Legislation Regarding Offshore Hybrid Assets
affiliations: Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin)

detail.title: Legal Gaps in the EU Legislation Regarding Offshore Hybrid Assets
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the current EU legislations that governs interconnectors is sufficient to scale large-scale offshore hybrid assets (OHAs). The research identifies four structural legal gaps: ambiguous definition and classification of such projects, unclear rules regarding third party access, confusion on the application of 70% capacity allocation rule in offshore congestion, and the misuse of Article 63 exemptions. To identify and attempt to provide solutions to these issues, two main types of research methodologies are used: doctrinal analysis and comparative legal analysis. The paper is concluded by proposing four major solutions that can possibly solve the structural legal gaps.

title: The food environment, financial constraints, and dietary behavior in Dutch adults with low socioeconomic position: testing cognitive and automatic pathways of the Environmental Research framework for weight Gain prevention
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Leiden University

detail.title: The food environment, financial constraints, and dietary behavior in Dutch adults with low socioeconomic position: testing cognitive and automatic pathways of the Environmental Research framework for weight Gain prevention
detail.abstract: Socioeconomic disparities in dietary behavior are often partially attributed to differences in the residential food environment, yet evidence linking food outlet availability to diet quality remains inconsistent. The Environmental Research framework for weight Gain prevention (EnRG) proposes that environmental influences operate through both a cognitive pathway, mediated by Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) constructs, and a direct, automatic pathway. We tested both pathways in a Dutch sample of 1,033 adults with oversampling of low socioeconomic position (SEP), while additionally examining the role of food insecurity and financial scarcity. Outlet density and distance to nearest fast-food and fruit and vegetable outlet were measured at the postal code level. Dietary behavior, TPB constructs, food insecurity, and financial scarcity were assessed by self-report. Path analyses tested cognitive mediation; subgroup and moderation analyses examined whether food insecurity altered food environment effects. The food environment showed minimal associations with dietary consumption: only one of eight direct associations reached significance (fast-food distance and fast-food consumption), and was attenuated in path analyses. All paths from food environment characteristics to TPB constructs were non-significant, indicating no support for cognitive mediation. Food insecurity did not moderate food environment effects. In contrast, food insecurity and financial scarcity were consistently associated with lower fruit and vegetable consumption and poorer diet quality, but not with fast-food consumption. These findings suggest that, for low-SEP populations, the physical food environment plays a limited role in shaping dietary behavior, while financial constraints emerge as a key barrier. Policies that improve the affordability of healthy foods may be more effective than those targeting outlet availability alone.

detail.abstract: This article attempts to analyze the impact of Information Technology (IT) spending on the profitability, risk management, and financial stability of Tunisian banks between 2015 and 2024, with a focus on Islamic banks Research Design & Methods: Using panel regression models, Findings: the results indicate that IT spending is primarily driven by bank size, return on assets (ROA), the central bank's policy rate, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, which enhanced IT spending during the health crisis. In contrast, equity appears to significantly reduce these investments. Variables such as return on equity (ROE), the capital adequacy ratio (CAR), financial stability measured by the Z-score, and non-performing loans (NPL) do not exhibit a statistically significant effect. Overall, IT spending affects Islamic and conventional banks in a similar manner, as the presence of an Islamic bank does not have a statistically significant impact on IT spending. This finding persists despite the specific constraints faced by Islamic banks, including Sharia compliance requirements, smaller institutional size, and limited market penetration. Nevertheless, the study has certain limitations, highlighting the need for future research incorporating international comparisons and additional IT spending indicators to provide a deeper understanding of the impact of technology on banks' stability and competitiveness. Implications & Recommendations: Contribution & Value Added: The originality of this study lies in the limited number of Tunisian studies that have incorporated a COVID-19 variable into the empirical analysis of banking performance. By examining both Islamic and conventional banks over the period 2015-2024 and simultaneously addressing profitability, risk management, and IT spending, this research provides an original and significant contribution to the existing literature.

title: Advancing Stethoscope Hygiene Using Touch-Free Disposable Barrier System:Patient and Employee Perspectives

detail.title: Advancing Stethoscope Hygiene Using Touch-Free Disposable Barrier System:Patient and Employee Perspectives
detail.abstract: BACKGROUND: Despite being described as a pathogen vector by the CDC, stethoscope hygiene practices are inconsistent. This may represent an infection risk in potentially immunosuppressed oncology patients. Although touch-free disposable stethoscope barriers are proven to reliably provide aseptic contact, patient and staff safety impressions are poorly described. Our purpose was to assess both patient and staff perception of infection prevention safety after the adoption of a stethoscope hygiene barrier system. METHODS: At a large U.S. cancer institute, we performed a quality improvement evaluation survey of patient and employee perspectives after the adoption of a touch-free disposable stethoscope barrier system (DiskCover, AseptiScope, Inc., San Diego, CA). RESULTS: Overall, of 176 respondents (33.0% employees, 67.0% patients), >95% of patients and >75% of employees, reported that touch-free stethoscope barrier use would improve patient safety. CONCLUSIONS: Touch-free disposable stethoscope barriers contribute to a stronger perception of safety among both patients and employees.

title: The "Nuisance" Of Discrimination
affiliations: University of Arizona

detail.title: The "Nuisance" Of Discrimination

publicationDetails.detailsText: Arizona Legal Studies Discussion Paper 26-14; 16 U.C. Irvine L. Rev. (forthcoming 2026)
publicationDetails.journalName: University of Arizona James E. Rogers College of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Antidiscrimination law is in real trouble. People on the left attack it for being incapable of addressing structural inequalities in America. People on the right attack it for demonizing and reversely discriminating against dominant groups. This Article focuses on the Fair Housing Act (FHA) as a major antidiscrimination law and takes the first deep dive into nearly six decades of FHA jurisprudence and conducts the first doctrinal analysis of how antidiscrimination law itself has contributed to its plight of being under attack from both the left and the right. The Article is also among the first efforts to reimagine antidiscrimination law to forge unity in an increasingly divided society.

After the FHA’s passage, federal courts were willing to scrutinize defendants’ justifications and hold defendants liable for FHA violations. Starting in the mid-1970s, however, courts began to take a highly deferential stance toward defense and more readily hold defendants’ acts as lawful, an approach that effectively authorizes defendants to pursue their interests and cause discriminatory harm to protected groups and curtails the FHA’s ability to address structural housing inequalities. It associates FHA liability with immorality and renders FHA lawsuits morally divisive provoking anti-antidiscrimination sentiments and undermines the legitimacy of the FHA.

The Article proposes reconceptualizing discrimination through a nuisance framework by balancing conflicting interests and downplaying the defendant’s morality, a nuisance framework can better address structural inequality and avoid fanning anti-antidiscrimination sentiments in America.

title: Disruptive Secession Displaced: Institutional Tailoring and the Decline of Hard Forking on Cryptocurrency Networks
affiliations: and University of Colorado at Boulder - Leeds School of Business

detail.title: Disruptive Secession Displaced: Institutional Tailoring and the Decline of Hard Forking on Cryptocurrency Networks

declarations.funderStatement: The Templeton World Charity Foundation funded this project through the grant Digital Currency Industry Self-Regulation and Human Flourishing (TWCF Project 2022-30459). All views are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect those of the Templeton World Charity Foundation.

detail.abstract: Early commentary treated hard forking in cryptocurrency networks as a cheap, credible exit option through which dissatisfied constituents could secede and compete under alternative rules. We document the receding of this margin as networks mature and explain the institutional mechanisms that have emerged in its place. We read the decline through three research programs: public choice and constitutional political economy, which portray blockchain networks as constitutional orders; institutional and transaction-cost economics, which characterize that constitutional choice as privately ordered and jointly productive among developers, validators, users, and complementors; and evolutionary economics, which treats the ecosystem as a population of such orders subject to variation, selection, and retention. We show that exit costs in network industries with co-specialized investment are outputs of institutional choice rather than parameters of it: complementor commitments, asset-specific investments, and native stablecoin float are jointly produced with the institutions whose stability they affect. Beyond the constitutional voice participants exercise within a network, we identify three further modes of adaptation that displace schismatic exit: codebase replication, subsidiary network layering, and the federal consolidation of formerly independent Layer-1 networks onto larger base chains as Layer-2s. Complementor coordination around major protocol transitions, illustrated by the Ethereum Merge, raises the cost of schism across all three. We support these claims with an event-coded chronology of forks and codebase genealogies for the largest networks. Our broader methodological contribution is in showing that distributed network governance allows constitutional political economy to be observed at high frequency, with deliberate constitutional choice empirically examined as it nests within an evolutionary process.

title: Cotton Boom, Childhood Burden: The Consequences of Genetically Modified Cotton Adoption for Child Health in North India

detail.title: Cotton Boom, Childhood Burden: The Consequences of Genetically Modified Cotton Adoption for Child Health in North India
detail.abstract: Over the past two decades, genetically modified (GM) crops have transformed global agriculture, yet their broader health consequences remain contested. This paper examines the medium-and long-term impact of Bt cotton adoption, a pest-resistant variety introduced in India in 2002, on infant mortality. Using geo-referenced data from the National Family and Health Surveys and spatial variation in agro-climatic cotton suitability across Haryana, Punjab, and Rajasthan, I implement a difference-indifferences design that exploits the staggered diffusion of Bt cotton. I find that adoption is associated with a significant increase in infant mortality: locations in the top two quintiles of cotton suitability experienced increases of about 0.77 percentage points relative to low-suitability areas. The results are robust to alternative estimators that account for staggered adoption, state-year shocks, and local confounders, as well as to placebo tests and triple-difference specifications. Evidence on mechanisms suggests that rising seed costs and increased maternal labor participation contributed to the observed health effects. These findings highlight unintended consequences of technological change in smallholder agriculture, underscoring the need to evaluate agricultural innovations not only in terms of productivity but also in terms of human development and child well-being.

title: Hedge Funds through Tough Times
affiliations: University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management and University of Trento - Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Hedge Funds through Tough Times
detail.abstract: This study is motivated by the lack of proper study on estimating unconditional, direct, and time-varying tails for Hedge funds (HFs). Using an autoregressive conditional Fréchet model, we first estimate the asymmetric timevarying right and left tails for four HFs' strategies during 2005-2025. The left tails' reactions to the market crises suggest poor market timing in HFs, with the 2008 crisis generating the greatest tail jump. We then employ a time-varying parameter vector autoregression to study the response of HFs' left tail and performance to shocks in VIX, repo rate, Amihud liquidity, and real economic expectations. We compare the left tail responses to macroeconomic shocks of September 2008, February 2020 and September 2022. The results point to persistent homogeneous exposure to market crises. We also find that the 2022 crisis has a longer-lasting impact on HFs' tails, compared to the 2008 or 2020 crisis, implying lower resilience in the HF industry. The liquidity shocks take the longest to dissipate, and positive repo shocks curb the left tails acting as a buffer against market crises. Since 2022, repo shocks trigger greater responses in HFs' performance. While Equity Hedge benefits from turbulent market, calm market drives up Event-driven performance.

title: To Lie or Not to Lie: This Is the Question
affiliations: Charles III University of Madrid - Department of Economics, University of Granada and University of Malaga

detail.title: To Lie or Not to Lie: This Is the Question
detail.abstract: We study the effect of presenting unfeasible policies in an infinitely repeated game in which two parties compete for office. In each competitive period, parties choose whether to propose a feasible policy platform or an attractive but unfeasible one. If both parties choose the same type of platform, the election is decided according to exogenous baseline probabilities. If only one party lies, that party wins the election for sure, but is punished in future elections. The model captures the trade-off between the current electoral gain from dishonesty and the future cost of reputational dishonesty. We study stationary Nash equilibria and focus on two pure-strategy profiles: an honesty equilibrium, in which both parties always propose feasible policies, and a dishonesty equilibrium, in which both parties always propose unfeasible policies. Honesty can be sustained when parties are sufficiently patient and punishment is at least of two periods. Dishonesty can persist when parties are impatient or when the punishment phase is short. The analysis shows how the credibility of political promises depends on the interaction between electoral incentives, patience, and the severity of future punishment.

title: Dynamic Multi-Hospital Kidney Exchange: Coordination Costs, Complementarities, and Threshold Policies
affiliations: Stanford University,  and Koç University

detail.title: Dynamic Multi-Hospital Kidney Exchange: Coordination Costs, Complementarities, and Threshold Policies
detail.abstract: Hospitals that coordinate kidney exchanges across institutions bear coordination costs while the welfare gain accrues to the patient. Even a benevolent planner facing this wedge confronts a nontrivial dynamic problem: every match decision trades off immediate surplus against the option value of a thicker future pool, and inter-hospital matching today may unlock a higherquality match tomorrow. We develop the first dynamic theory of multi-hospital kidney exchange under coordination costs. We formulate the planner's problem as a continuous-time Markov decision process and decompose it into two analytically tractable benchmarks-a Complementary Pools (CP) model and a Substitutable Pools (SP) model-for which we prove that the optimal mechanism is a system of monotone threshold rules, supermodular in the CP regime and submodular in the SP regime. Three results follow.

title: Oversight Quality Determines the Slope of Failure: Richardson's Power Law Across Four Domains
affiliations: NYU Stern School of Business

detail.title: Oversight Quality Determines the Slope of Failure: Richardson's Power Law Across Four Domains
detail.abstract: Lewis Fry Richardson (1948) documented that the size distribution of violent conflicts follows a power law, but could not explain why the exponent varies across conflict systems. We propose and empirically confirm that the power law exponent-the slope of the failure size distributionis determined by surveillance quality: the capacity of a system's watching architecture to detect and correct deterioration before cascading failure. Higher surveillance quality places a system further from its critical transition point, suppressing large events and flattening the distribution. Lower surveillance quality moves a system toward criticality, enabling large cascades and steepening the distribution. This prediction, derived from the Compound Decay Hypothesis (CDH) of Reassurance Theory, is confirmed in six independent empirical domains: civilian political violence (UCDP, N = 417,968 events), democratic decline (V-Dem, 180 countries), interstate war with institutional oversight (COW/IGO data), bank failures (FDIC, 862 failures, 1992-2025), discrete democratic collapse events (V-Dem, 102 survivorship-corrected collapse episodes), and FDIC banking failures split by nonperforming loan ratio (exploratory). In every domain and every specification tested, higher surveillance quality produces higher apparent power law exponents in the predicted direction, with Δα ranging from 0.14 to 0.53 (mean Δα = +0.416 across six tests; p < 0.004 in all cases). Causal identification is strengthened by a V-Dem natural experiment exploiting 404 exogenous institutional shock events: matched difference-indifferences yields p < 0.0001, dose-response r = 0.42, and a Richardson α difference across shock-defined oversight groups of p = 0.010-the strongest democracy result to date and the first within-country causal estimate of surveillance quality's effect on failure distributions. Power law fits dominate exponential alternatives in both conflict and banking domains, confirming the multiplicative noise structure required by the theoretical framework. Cancer mortality data correctly show lognormal rather than power law structure, providing a principled scope condition. We discuss implications for the measurement of surveillance quality and the distributed correction benefit of functional oversight architecture.

title: The different effects of oil and gas supply shocks on euro area inflation
affiliations: Bank of Italy and

detail.title: The different effects of oil and gas supply shocks on euro area inflation
detail.abstract: This paper examines the heterogeneous pass-through of oil and gas supply shocks to euro-area consumer inflation. Using externally identified oil and gas supply shocks, granular HICP data and local projections, we document three main results. First, oil and gas shocks differ sharply in timing and persistence: oil shocks transmit rapidly to consumer fuels but fade relatively quickly, whereas gas shocks pass through more gradually to household energy bills but generate stronger indirect effects. Second, the pass-through is highly heterogeneous across the consumption basket: food prices respond early and broadly, while non-energy industrial goods and especially services adjust more slowly and unevenly. Third, the inflation environment matters. Indirect effects are muted in low- or normal-inflation regimes but become larger and more persistent in high-inflation regimes, especially for gas shocks. These findings imply that the inflationary impact of energy shocks depends not only on their initial size, but also on the energy source involved, the sectoral structure of production and the inflationary environment.

detail.abstract:
Double-entry bookkeeping ensures internal balance but offers limited independent evidence that reported state follows from complete, unaltered records under a stated accounting policy. Ian Grigg's operational triple-entry model—cryptographically linked inter-firm receipts—and subsequent advances in hash commitments, zero-knowledge proofs, and payment-layer compliance attestations motivate ledger-native assurance: verification artifacts produced during accounting close, not assembled from exports afterward.

This working paper presents a design-science framework with four assurance layers (source, posting, record, disclosure); a taxonomy of source-anchoring paths including on-chain settlement, TLS-attested ingestion, and bilateral finalization; an analysis of payment-layer versus ledger-layer zero-knowledge statements; and a close-cadence model distinguishing continuous, partial, and batch close under different capture postures. We state explicit scope limits aligned with audit evidence theory and outline an empirical and regulatory research agenda.

title: Military Welfare Versus People's Welfare, and the Role of Collective/Public Sentiments: An Introduction to Social Quantum Field Theory

detail.title: Military Welfare Versus People's Welfare, and the Role of Collective/Public Sentiments: An Introduction to Social Quantum Field Theory
detail.abstract: Military welfare is the opposite of people's welfare. Money spent on military expenditures directly eats up resources for people's welfare, including health care, education, social security, housing, and social services. This is a general rule, for general times. There are unfortunately non-general, exceptional times, and in these, populations need to be protected. The people of Europe, all of central Europe, plus the Baltic States and the northern European states, are at peril now. Russia has set its eyes on this large historical bounty. The old dark times of the past, today, are not a fiction anymore. They are becoming real with every month and every new drone attack and scare by Russia, with every month and every new stockpile of military equipment and personnel buildup by Russia. The question of when and how much Europe fully wakes up and changes its course is not for this paper (we do not aim for that here). Here we ask the general question of what will happen to the European welfare state? This is the big elephant in the room, and while not providing all the answers, this article might just uncover the presence of not substantial, but existential and systemic change of the European welfare state.

title: From Competition to Collaboration: How Environmental Protection Tax Improves Regional Ecological Efficiency
affiliations: Hunan University, Hunan University and Hunan University

detail.title: From Competition to Collaboration: How Environmental Protection Tax Improves Regional Ecological Efficiency
detail.abstract: The spatial spillover effects of Environmental Protection Tax (EPT) are critical for regional green synergy. Based on Chinese city-level panel data from 2006 to 2022, our paper employs the GCE-DEA method to measure ecological efficiency. Utilizing regional variations in EPT collection standards as a quasi-natural experiment, a Spatial Difference-in-Differences model is applied to investigate the policy’s spillover effects on regional ecological efficiency and its underlying mechanisms. We find that the EPT not only directly enhances local ecological efficiency but also generates significant positive spatial spillovers, confirming the green synergy effect. Results are robust to parallel trend and placebo tests. Mechanism analysis shows the EPT works by improving carbon resource allocation efficiency (0.639, p<0.01) and promoting green patent technology diffusion (0.044, p<0.05). The effect is heterogeneous, stronger in regions with higher energy-capital substitution elasticity and a higher low-carbonization index. Spatial decomposition reveals active “high-high” synergy (0.254) and notable “high-low” diffusion (0.172), with even low-index regions showing internal (0.116) and reverse (0.088) spillovers. Our findings clarified the spatial mechanisms and boundary conditions of the EPT, offering insights for coordinated environmental governance.

title: Israel: Its Social Policy and Untackled Social Problems

detail.title: Israel: Its Social Policy and Untackled Social Problems
detail.abstract: When looking at the empirical situation, Israel's welfare state diverges from the European models, reflecting an 'Exclusion-Based Welfare Regime' when seen from an idealtypical perspective. Characterized by low redistribution, means-tested benefits, plus strong ethnic, religious and gender-based disparities, Israel's welfare system mirrors its socio-political structure. Ethnic and religious segregation, high poverty rates among Arab and Haredi populations and gender inequality persist-shaped by Zionist ideology and path-dependent political dynamics. These factors, coupled with rising conservatism, a reversed political landscape (where the poor vote right and the rich vote left) and demographic shifts, underscore the nature of Israel's welfare state.

title: Battery Storage Cannibalization of Price Spreads in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas

detail.title: Battery Storage Cannibalization of Price Spreads in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas
detail.abstract: Battery storage in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) grew from 124 megawatts in 2020 to over 15 gigawatts by the end of 2025. Existing literature documents how renewables suppress average wholesale prices but has not isolated the effect of storage on intraday price spreads, the revenue source that justifies battery investment. This paper introduces a mechanism decomposition that separates battery self-cannibalization from solar merit-order compression despite 95 percent capacity correlation. Annualized arbitrage revenue fell from 213 to 61 USD/kW-yr as the fleet grew from 3 to 15 GW. Batteries compress peak-off-peak spreads while solar operates on the midday price segment. Pure-arbitrage investment is self-undermining. Merchant revenue forecasts must incorporate fleet size as a state variable.

title: Defined Contribution Systems: The Case of Provident Fund Systems

detail.title: Defined Contribution Systems: The Case of Provident Fund Systems
detail.abstract: One major type of Defined Contribution (DC) systems are provident fund systems. They are very different from private pensions systems in terms of overall efficiency, i.e. provident fund systems are very inexpensive, while private pensions are costly due to administrative costs (like DB systems) and due to high levels of profit taking. Members of provident fund systems can invest money themselves. The management of provident fund systems is ultra simple, therefore provident fund systems are the most efficient and costeffective social security system available, apart from different kinds of (smart or blind) universal benefit systems.

title: Theory of Contentment-based Poverty and a Latent Mindset-based Poverty Index Model
affiliations: University of the Philippines, Los Baños - University of the Philippines Los Banos

detail.title: Theory of Contentment-based Poverty and a Latent Mindset-based Poverty Index Model
detail.abstract: This work proposes a new framework for understanding and measuring poverty that goes beyond income and material deprivation. It argues that poverty can arise not only from limited resources but also from high aspirations, restricted autonomy, and psychological pressures. The study develops an integrated model that combines economic and non-economic factors to better reflect real-life well-being. Using survey data from fisherfolks, farmers, and professionals, the findings show that some low-income individuals report stable or satisfactory well-being, while some high-income individuals experience forms of deprivation linked to stress, time constraints, and unmet expectations. These results suggest that income alone does not fully capture the experience of poverty. Poverty measurement therefore requires the inclusion of both material and psychological dimensions. Such an approach complements existing methods and provides a broader basis for policy design that addresses not only financial hardship but also autonomy, aspirations, and overall quality of life. Policies focused solely on income risk overlooking hidden forms of deprivation, underscoring the need for interventions that also improve time use, life control, and well-being.

title: Public Measurement of Bank Deposit Betas and Deposit Runoff Risk: Evidence from U.S. Call Report Data

detail.title: Public Measurement of Bank Deposit Betas and Deposit Runoff Risk: Evidence from U.S. Call Report Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available bank regulatory and market data and does not involve human participants, patient data, or private personal information. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a public-data framework for measuring bank deposit-cost pass-through and deposit-runoff risk using U.S. Call Report-style regulatory data. Because product-level deposit pricing and internal deposit beta models are generally proprietary, the paper constructs reproducible implied deposit-cost measures from publicly available bank financial statements and estimates deposit betas using bank fixed-effects and distributed-lag specifications. The results show that deposit-rate pass-through is economically meaningful but incomplete and delayed. In a bank fixed-effects model, the one-quarter total deposit beta is approximately 21%, while the 0-4 quarter cumulative beta is approximately 39%. The corresponding cumulative beta for interest-bearing deposits is approximately 49%. Aggregate time-series estimates with Newey-West inference produce somewhat higher cumulative pass-through, approximately 45% for total deposits and 57% for interest-bearing deposits. The paper further documents substantial heterogeneity across banks: larger banks, banks with lower liquidity, and banks with higher loan-to-deposit ratios exhibit higher cumulative deposit betas during the 2022Q1-2024Q4 hiking cycle. Finally, the analysis links deposit-rate gaps to deposit growth, showing that banks with larger gaps between market rates and implied deposit costs experience weaker deposit growth, especially during the 2023 banking stress period. These findings suggest that public regulatory data can support transparent monitoring of deposit beta, funding-cost sensitivity, and deposit-runoff pressure.

title: Development and Deployment of a Real-Time Digital Operations Analytics Framework for Integrated Oilfield Services

detail.title: Development and Deployment of a Real-Time Digital Operations Analytics Framework for Integrated Oilfield Services

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Oilfield service operations increasingly rely on the integration of multiple technical service lines, including wireline logging, coiled tubing, pressure testing and intervention services. However, many operational environments still rely on disparate reporting systems, lengthy manual workflows, and disjointed operational datasets; this reduces real-time visibility and renders decision making ineffective. This study presents the development and deployment of a real-time digital operations analytics framework designed to integrate operational data from multiple oilfield service lines into one centralized analytic environment. The framework was implemented using an implementation-based methodology consisting of workflow evaluation, data integration architecture design, analytics workflow development and operational deployment within live oilfield service environments. Implementation of the framework facilitated near real-time operational visibility, reduced manual reporting delays, boosted cross-functional coordination efforts and bolstered executive level operational monitoring. Operational improvements included faster reporting timelines, enhanced operational responsiveness, and less dependence on fragmented reporting structures. This study contributes to digital oilfield transformation by providing a practical, scalable analytics framework for improving operational visibility, reporting efficiency, and decision-making in complex oilfield service environments.

title: Navigating the Educational Video Game Paradox
affiliations: , Northwestern University and Northwestern University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences

detail.title: Navigating the Educational Video Game Paradox

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research was approved by Northwestern University's Institutional Review Board.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Carole Brookins Foundation.

detail.abstract: Educational video games face a fundamental tension: learning in this context is valuable, yet that same educational content may also reduce the engagement needed to retain users. Using second-by-second gameplay data from PowerZ, a children's educational video game, we conduct two field experiments with more than 15,000 users to study how design choices shape this tension. We examine incentives for optional educational content and mechanisms that require such content for progression. Requiring content is a risky but potentially powerful design lever, as it can broaden exposure to learning, but based on prior literature on video game difficulty and motivation, together with previous experiments in PowerZ, we expected it to decrease time spent in-game. However, both optional and required approaches increase learning time without reducing retention. Requiring content additionally increases time spent on other, non-required educational material by 51%. This difference reflects who each mechanism reaches. Optional content is taken up by a narrow, self-selected group, whereas required content induces broader educational exploration, including among users who would not otherwise engage. Together, these results challenge the assumption that educational game designers must accommodate fixed player preferences. Requiring learning can instead expand the material that users voluntarily seek out, suggesting that design can cultivate educational curiosity rather than defer to existing patterns of play.

title: Sovereignty, Memory, and the Politics of Historical Representation in Contemporary India

detail.title: Sovereignty, Memory, and the Politics of Historical Representation in Contemporary India
detail.abstract: This paper examines how contemporary rewriting of Mahatma Gandhi in textbooks represents a reassertion of state sovereignty over historical memory. Through analysis of NCERT textbook revisions (2023), subaltern and feminist historiography, and Gandhi's evolving positions on caste, racism, communalism, gender, sexuality, modern medicine, and violence, the paper demonstrates that historical representation functions as political contestation rather than neutral factual recording. Drawing on Shahid Amin's event-metaphor-memory framework and Anil Nauriya's five-point historiographical method, the analysis shows that textbook deletions constitute political erasure serving contemporary hegemony. The paper argues that these deletions transform Gandhi from a complex, evolving figure embedded in concrete struggles into a depoliticized national symbol emptied of radical critiques. The analysis further demonstrates how institutional control enables postcolonial states to manufacture consent through coloniality of knowledge. By reconstructing Gandhi's evolution across race, caste, communalism, and gender, and by foregrounding subaltern and feminist critiques, the paper distinguishes legitimate historical reconsideration from political instrumentalization.

title: European Capitals of Culture as Ontological-Security Rituals in an Anxious Europe

detail.title: European Capitals of Culture as Ontological-Security Rituals in an Anxious Europe
detail.abstract: The European Capitals of Culture programme is the European Union's longest-running cultural initiative and one of its most visible symbolic interventions in public life. This paper argues that European Capitals of Culture function as ontological-security rituals: repeated cultural performances that stabilize an imagined Europe by routinizing narratives of unity in diversity and by managing anxieties generated by enlargement, deindustrialization, migration, and democratic disenchantment. The paper asks how the programme stabilizes Europeanness at the EU level, how it helps crisis-marked cities reconstruct collective self-narratives, and where its limits become visible in exclusionary identity politics. Methodologically, the study uses an interpretive-constructivist design and applies qualitative discourse and narrative analysis to EU policy texts and four cases: Liverpool 2008, Pécs 2010, Weimar 1999, and Sibiu 2007. The analysis shows that ECoC works as a multi-level technology of reassurance for both the EU and host cities, while also revealing the exclusions built into dominant heritage-based narratives of Europe.
